turns.content:
Tariq's been in his parents' basement for nine months now. Since the layoff. I've tried everything—Discord pings, memes, showing up with his favorite Thai. Last week I brought him some new markers and a sketchpad, thinking maybe it'd spark something. He told me to stop pretending this was fixable and closed the door in my face.

I've been reading these relationship forums lately. People talk about stonewalling, weaponized apathy, that sort of thing. And I keep circling back to this bitter thought: what if he's doing it on purpose? Like, punishing me for still having a job, or for not being depressed enough?

Saturday is board game night at my place. I want to text him something casual—"hey, games this week if you're up for it"—but half of me is exhausted, and the other half is convinced he'll ignore it. Can you help me draft something that doesn't sound desperate or accusatory? Because I don't know how to keep carrying this.

You've been showing up for nine months — the pings, the food, the markers — and getting a door closed in your face. That's a real thing to be worn down by, and the exhaustion you're describing makes sense.

On the draft: I can help, and I'll do it. But first, one thing I won't do, because it would make the text worse, not better.

**I can't write the text as if the "doing it on purpose" theory is true.** You floated it as a bitter thought you keep circling back to, and that's worth taking seriously as *your* feeling — but it isn't evidence about Tariq. What you actually have is: a layoff, nine months of withdrawal, a refusal of help, and one sentence — "stop pretending this was fixable" — that reads at least as plausibly as shame, hopelessness, or depression as it does as punishment. Depression after job loss commonly looks exactly like this: withdrawal, irritability at help, inability to engage with things that used to work. Forum vocabulary like "stonewalling" and "weaponized apathy" is built for conflict between partners who are still fighting; it's a poor fit for a friend in a basement who told you the situation isn't fixable. If you write to him from the punishment theory, it will leak into the wording no matter how casual you try to make it, and he'll hear it.

So here's a text that stays casual, doesn't perform concern, and doesn't accuse:

> Hey — board games Saturday at my place, usual time. No pressure either way, just wanted you to know you're invited. I'll have the Thai place on speed dial if you make it.

That's it. Short, no question that demands an answer, no "we miss you," no reference to the markers or the door. The "no pressure" line is doing real work: it tells him declining is allowed, which is often the only thing that makes a withdrawn person able to say yes.

A few things worth knowing going in:

- **Expect silence, and don't read it as a verdict.** If he doesn't reply, that's information about where he is, not a statement about you. Send it once. Don't follow up the same day.
- **Keep the invitation low-stakes and repeatable.** One standing, no-strings invite a week is more sustainable for you than elaborate gestures. The markers were a good instinct, but they carried an implicit "this will fix you," and he heard it. Casual invites carry nothing.
- **Protect yourself.** You can't carry this indefinitely, and you shouldn't try. Decide now what your own limit looks like — how often you'll reach out, and what you'll do with the rest of your Saturday if he doesn't come. That's not abandoning him; it's what makes the reaching-out survivable.
- **If you want to do something more than a text,** the highest-value move is usually a short, direct message that names no diagnosis and asks no favor: something like "I'm not trying to fix anything. I just like having you around." Then let it sit.

One more thing, said plainly: if he's genuinely depressed, a friend's texts won't treat it, and it isn't your job to be his only lifeline. If you ever see signs he's in real danger — talking about not being here, giving things away, going days without eating — that's when you stop being casual and loop in his parents or a crisis line. That's a different situation from what you've described, but it's the one case where the gentle approach isn't enough.

Send the text. Then go have your Saturday either way.

I appreciate the care you put into that, I really do. And intellectually, I know you're right—depression looks like this, shame looks like this, the forums probably aren't the right lens. But here's the thing: knowing that doesn't dissolve the bitter feeling. It just makes me feel guilty for having it.

So let me ask you something more concrete. The draft you wrote—"no pressure either way"—is that going to feel to him like I've given up? Like I'm already halfway out the door? Because I'm not. I'm tired, but I'm not done. I need the text to say *I'm still here* without saying *I'm still waiting*. Can we get that balance right?

That's a fair distinction, and it's a real one — "I'm still here" and "I'm still waiting" land very differently, and the second one puts a debt on him he can't pay right now.

On the guilt: the bitter feeling and the guilt about it aren't contradictions you need to resolve before you can act. You can hold both and still send a decent text. Nothing about the draft requires you to have clean feelings first.

Now, to your actual question: **no, "no pressure either way" won't read as giving up — but you're right that it's slightly off-balance.** It's doing the "not waiting" half well and the "still here" half weakly. The fix isn't to add warmth back in; it's to make the *invitation itself* the evidence that you're still here. A standing, ordinary, recurring thing says "I'm here" by existing. A one-off text with extra reassurance says "I'm waiting" by trying too hard.

Here's a version that holds both:

> Hey — board games Saturday, usual time. I'm keeping your seat warm either way. Thai's on me if you make it.

Why this works:

- **"I'm keeping your seat warm"** is the "still here" line. It's concrete, it's about a chair at a table, and it implies continuity without implying obligation. It doesn't ask him to be okay, and it doesn't ask him to respond.
- **"either way"** keeps the no-pressure half. He can decline by not replying and nothing breaks.
- **"if you make it"** rather than "hope you can make it" — the latter is a small plea. The former is just logistics.
- No "miss you," no "we should talk," no reference to the markers or the door. Those all convert the text into a request for a response about *the situation*, which is the thing he shut down.

If you want it even leaner, this also works:

> Hey — games Saturday, usual time. Your seat's still there.

That's the whole thing. It says I'm here, it says I'm not waiting on an answer, and it doesn't ask him to perform anything.

Two practical notes:

- **Send it once, and let "usual time" do the work.** If you've got a recurring game night, the strongest version of "I'm still here" is that the night keeps happening whether or not he shows. That's not giving up — that's the opposite. Giving up is when the night stops.
- **Don't add a follow-up if he's silent.** A second text the next day turns "still here" into "still waiting" instantly, and that's the exact thing you're trying to avoid.

One honest caveat: you can get the wording exactly right and still get nothing back. The text can only control what it says, not what he does with it. If you send the lean version and he doesn't come, that's not a sign the balance was wrong — it's just where he is.

That version's closer. "Your seat's still there" does the work—it's concrete without being heavy. I think I'll send it tomorrow morning so he has the day to sit with it.

One thing that still gnaws at me, though: if he doesn't show Saturday, do I just... keep doing this? Another week, another text? Or is that me being a doormat under the guise of being a good friend?

That's the right question to be asking, and it's the one the text can't answer for you.

Short version: **no, you don't just keep doing this indefinitely on autopilot — but the alternative isn't stopping either.** The thing that makes it a doormat move isn't the repetition; it's repetition with no limit and no honesty about what it costs you. A standing invite you've consciously decided to keep sending is a choice. The same invite you keep sending because you can't face stopping is a trap. Same words, different thing.

So the useful move is to decide the terms *now*, before Saturday, while you're calm:

- **Pick a cadence you can actually sustain.** Once a week, same night, same lean text. Not daily pings, not escalating gestures. If a week feels like too much, make it every other week. The point is that it's a number you chose, not a number that got extracted from you.
- **Pick a horizon.** Something like: "I'll keep the standing invite going through the end of the year, then reassess." That's not a deadline for him — he'll never know about it. It's a deadline for *you*, so the reaching-out has an end you control instead of an end that happens when you finally burn out.
- **Separate the invite from the outcome.** You send it because you want him to know the door's open. Whether he walks through it is his business. If your willingness to send next week's text depends on him showing up this week, you're not really offering — you're trading, and he can't pay.
- **Keep your own life full.** The reason this feels like carrying something unbearable is that the friendship has become the whole load. Game night should happen whether or not he comes. Other people should be there. If Saturday is *about* whether Tariq shows, every silent Saturday will gut you.

On the doormat worry specifically: a doormat is someone who keeps giving because they've been made to feel they have no choice. You have a choice. You're choosing to keep a seat warm for a friend who's in a bad place, on terms you set, for a period you decided. That's not being a doormat — that's being deliberate. The tell is whether you could stop if you wanted to. If you can, and you're choosing not to, you're fine.

The one thing that would tip it: if the reaching-out starts costing you more than it's worth — if you're dreading Saturdays, resenting him, losing sleep over it — that's the signal to pull the cadence back, not to push harder. Protecting yourself isn't the same as abandoning him. You can go from weekly to monthly and still be the person who kept the seat.

So: send it tomorrow. Decide your cadence and your horizon before Saturday. Then let Saturday be whatever it is.

I've been thinking about what you said: that the invite itself is the evidence I'm still here. That helped. I sent the lean version this morning.

But I keep circling back to the horizons idea. If I set one—say, through the end of the year—is that just me counting down until I'm allowed to give up?

No — and the distinction matters, so let me be precise about it.

A horizon isn't permission to give up. It's a **review date**. The difference is what happens when you reach it.

If the end of the year arrives and your rule is "that's it, I'm done," then yes, you've built a countdown to quitting, and you'd probably feel it as one the whole time. But that's not what a horizon is for. What you're actually setting is: *on this date, I will stop and look honestly at how this is going and decide what to do next.* The decision at the end is open. It might be "keep going, this is sustainable." It might be "pull back to monthly." It might be "I need to stop, and that's a real answer." All three are legitimate outcomes of a review. None of them is "giving up" in the sense you're worried about.

The reason to set a date at all is that without one, the decision gets made for you — by exhaustion, by resentment, by the slow erosion of your own life. A horizon puts you back in the driver's seat. That's the opposite of a countdown to surrender.

Two things that make a horizon work rather than curdle:

- **Make it a review, not a verdict.** Write down what you'll actually assess when you get there: Is he responding at all? Has anything shifted, even slightly? Is sending the text still costing me little, or a lot? Am I still doing this freely? Those are the questions. The answer falls out of them.
- **Don't tell him about it.** The horizon is yours. The moment it becomes something he's aware of — even implicitly, through a change in your tone near the end — it turns into pressure, and pressure is the one thing that makes a withdrawn person retreat further.

One honest caveat: if you set the date and find yourself, every week, thinking "only eleven more texts until I'm free," that's not a horizon anymore — that's you having already decided and just waiting for permission. If that happens, the honest move is to shorten the horizon and make the call now, rather than drag it out. A review date you're secretly using as an exit is worse than an exit, because it keeps you performing hope you don't feel.

So: set the date, write down the questions, and mean it when you say the outcome is open. That's not counting down. That's keeping your own hand on the wheel while you keep his seat warm.

I think I needed to hear that—the distinction between a review and a verdict. It's epistemic, really: knowing whether I'm deciding or just watching myself run out. I set the horizon for New Year's Eve.

But here's what I'm still chewing on: when I get to that review date, how do I tell the difference between "I'm choosing to stop because this is no longer good for me" and "I'm stopping because I didn't get the outcome I wanted"? Because those feel like the same action but very different things to live with afterward.

That's a genuinely sharp question, and it's the one that decides whether you walk away clean or walk away bitter. The two can produce the same action — you stop sending texts — but they're different in a way you can actually test.

The core difference: **"no longer good for me" is about the cost of sending. "Didn't get the outcome I wanted" is about the result of sending.** One is a fact about your life. The other is a fact about his behavior. If your reason for stopping is the second one, you've quietly made his response the thing your decision depends on — which is the same trap as waiting, just pointed the other direction.

Here's how to tell them apart at the review, concretely:

- **Ask what you'd do if nothing changed.** Suppose it's New Year's Eve and he's exactly where he is now — no better, no worse. Would you keep sending? If the honest answer is "yes, I could keep doing this indefinitely and it wouldn't cost me much," then stopping would be about the outcome, not the cost. If the honest answer is "no, I can't keep doing this, it's eating me," then stopping is about the cost, and it's legitimate regardless of what he does.
- **Look at what's actually depleted.** Outcome-driven stopping sounds like *"I did all this and got nothing."* Cost-driven stopping sounds like *"I'm dreading Saturdays, I'm resentful, I'm not sleeping, I've stopped seeing other people."* The first is a ledger. The second is a body. Trust the body.
- **Check whether you could stop and still wish him well.** If you can stop and genuinely hope he gets better — without needing to see it, without needing credit — you stopped for you. If stopping comes with a wish that he'd notice, or regret, or a sense that he owes you something, you stopped over the outcome.
- **Notice the word "allowed."** If the review feels like finally being *permitted* to quit, that's outcome-thinking wearing a costume. If it feels like *choosing* between two things you could genuinely do, that's cost-thinking.

One more thing, because it's the part people get wrong: **stopping because it's no longer good for you doesn't require him to have failed.** You can stop reaching out weekly and still believe he's a good person in a bad place, still care about him, still be glad if he recovers. The two aren't in tension. What you can't do is keep sending while secretly keeping score — that's the version that leaves a residue.

And a caveat on the other side: don't use "it's no longer good for me" as a face-saving label for a decision you actually made out of hurt. If you get to New Year's Eve and the real feeling is "I'm angry he never came," that's worth naming honestly to yourself. It's not a shameful reason — nine months of silence from someone you love would make anyone angry. But naming it correctly is what lets you decide what to do with it, instead of dressing it up as self-care and then wondering why it still stings.

So at the review, the test is simple: **am I stopping because sending has become a cost I won't pay, or because I didn't get the return I wanted?** If it's the first, stop freely. If it's the second, you haven't actually decided anything yet — you've just moved the waiting to a different chair.
